newsitem.title: USA: U.S. gives Afghan embassy one week to close.
newsitem.headline: U.S. gives Afghan embassy one week to close.

text.p: The United States on Thursday gave the Afghan embassy in Washington one week to close down because it does not want to seem partial towards the fundamentalist Taleban, who control the Afghan capital.

"The Department of State has decided to suspend temporarily operations at the Afghanistan embassy in Washington, effective August 21st," State Department spokesman James Rubin told reporters at his daily briefing.
"We concluded that the result of not taking this action would be that one representative of the Taleban would end up being in charge -- that would send a signal that we were not neutral," he added.

"The department has been forced to take this action because of continuing contention among Afghan factions within the embassy ... and our belief that there is no effective government in the country," he said.

The Afghan embassy has had two senior diplomats in dispute over who represents the country. They are Seraj Jamal, nominated charge d'affaires by the Taleban, and former charge d'affaires Yar Mohammad Mohabbat, an appointee of the old government.
In May the Taleban asked Mohabbat to give up his post in favor of Jamal but the State Department has not accredited Jamal as his successor, an embassy source said.
The Taleban militia movement holds the capital Kabul but forces loyal to the old government of Burhaneddin Rabbani are fighting to regain power from the north of the country.

"You had a situation where one man (Jamal) was left standing in the Afghan embassy and we thought it would be a mistake to signal that that faction was someone we preferred or not," the spokesman said.

The Taleban have been widely criticized for their human rights record, especially their treatment of women. When they took Kabul last year they closed girls' schools and banned women from working except in the medical sector.
Rubin said the Afghan diplomats could stay in the United States as representatives of Afghan political factions but they would lose their diplomatic immunity.
"If they want to stay and serve as a faction representer, they would have to do it from some other place (outside the embassy building)," he added.

The Afghan consulate in New York can however stay open because it provides services to the Afghan-American community. "We draw a distinction between the political functions performed in an embassy and the service functions performed at a consulate," he said.
The embassy source said that Mohabbat left the embassy on Thursday and Jamal would start to travel in the hope of helping to form a broad-based Afghan government.
Rubin said the United States shared this objective.
"This suspension does not signify a break in relations nor any diminution of U.S. government interest in promoting a peace process that will lead to a broadly representative government," he said.
